paper_id: Qian et al. - 2014 - PADS Passive detection of moving targets with dynamic speed using PHY layer information
title: PADS: Passive Detection of Moving Targets with Dynamic Speed using PHY Layer Information
motivation: RSS-based detection fails for slow-moving targets since signal changes are buried by intrinsic RSS variance
problem_framing: Detect moving humans of dynamic speed using WiFi CSI without attaching devices to targets
key_insight: Phase information from CSI after linear transformation is more sensitive to slow motion than amplitude; eigenvalue-based features are power-irrelevant
method_signature: CSI phase sanitization + eigenvalue covariance feature + SVM + multi-antenna MIMO fusion
evaluation_criteria: True positive rate (detecting motion) and true negative rate (static correctly classified)
negative_result_or_admitted_limitation: RSSI-based approach reaches equally high performance but suffers from temporal variance and unstable performance
evidence_for_taste: RSS changes caused by especially slow and slight target movements would be buried by its intrinsic variances
we do derive a usable and effective feature of the true phase
the self-similarity within individual state is always remarkably smaller than cross-similarity
changes of phases are much more sensitive to slow human motion
one key reason is that all the features involved is power independent
thinking_moves: Phase was abandoned by prior work; prove it contains usable motion signal after denoising
Design features invariant to absolute power so system works without environment calibration
Reframe detection problem: phase changes detect slow motion where amplitude fails
Exploit spatial diversity from MIMO to reduce risk of selecting a 'bad' antenna
Even minimal human motion causes perceivable CSI perturbations enabling detection
extraction_notes: Venue not explicitly stated in paper text (likely IEEE PerCom based on references). Researcher Yunhao Liu is senior author (corresponding). Phase sanitization math partially clipped in source.
